claims.text: The onset and progression of the phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by thermally induced Cu surface segregation.
Cu surface segregation lowers the local melting temperature at the nanoparticle surface.
The lowered surface melting temperature initiates premelting that propagates inward as temperature rises.
As-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles initially have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Increasing temperature drives Cu atoms to segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other constituent elements.
Cu-enriched surface sites melt below the bulk melting point.
Surface premelting progresses inward and ultimately produces complete nanoparticle melting.
In situ TEM will show melting beginning at nanoparticle surfaces.
Locations where melting begins will coincide with Cu enrichment detected by EDS.
Pre-annealing produces a more homogenized surface and minimizes surface segregation.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles will exhibit a delayed or higher premelting or melting onset temperature relative to untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed behavior requires nanoparticle sizes that permit sufficient atomic mobility for segregation.
Extremely small nanoparticles may not follow the proposed segregation-mediated melting behavior.
Extremely rapid heating may suppress or alter the proposed segregation-mediated melting behavior.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during the experiment.
A lack of a statistically significant melting-onset delay in pre-annealed particles, or surface premelting without Cu enrichment, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The starting as-synthesized particles are described as already having a homogeneous elemental distribution, yet pre-annealing is assumed to make their surfaces more homogeneous and less segregated than those of untreated particles. The proposed comparison therefore lacks a clearly distinct initial segregation state.

Heating is asserted to drive Cu surface segregation, while pre-annealing—also a thermal treatment—is asserted to minimize segregation without a specified annealing temperature, duration, quench, or other process that would explain the opposite effect.
